Ubayy (Ubayy ibn Ka'b) recited (al-mutazammil) in its original form. Ikrimah recited it with the zay lightened, meaning "the one who wraps his body or himself." Some of the early scholars (al-salaf) recited it with the zay lightened and the mim fathah, meaning "the one who has been wrapped." Al-Zamakhshari has a discussion on how God called him with this description, but I struck it out and left it out of my book. Al-Suhayli said: "al-Muzzammil is not one of his names, peace be upon him, by which he is known. It is derived from the state he was in at the time of being addressed. When the Arabs wish to show tenderness to the one they address and leave out reproach, they call him by a name derived from the state he is in, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Ali, may Allah honour his face, when he was asleep and dust was clinging to his side: 'Get up, Abu Turab' (father of dust)." This indicates that he is being gentle with him. So His saying ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ contains affection and tenderness.

The majority recited ﴿qum al-layl﴾ with a kasra on the mim, following the original rule for joining two sukun letters. Abu al-Sammal recited it with a damma, to follow the vowel of the qaf. It was also read with a fathah, seeking lightness. Ibn Jinni said: "The purpose of the vowel is to avoid joining two sukun letters, so whichever vowel the letter takes achieves the aim. Qum is a command." The majority said: "It is on the basis of recommendation (nadb)." It was also said: "It was an obligation upon the Messenger alone," and it was said: "It was upon him and upon all of them." Qatadah said: "It continued for a year or two." Aisha said: "Eight months. Then Allah had mercy on them and the verse was revealed: ﴿Surely your Lord knows﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20] and the following verses, and He lightened it for them. ﴿Stand up at night, except a little.﴾"

The exception shows that the standing commanded covers the whole night, which is why the exception from it is valid. If it did not cover the whole night, the exception from it would not be valid. Standing for the whole night continuously is not possible, so He made an exception from it for the rest of the body. According to the Basrans, al-layl is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf), even though the verb covers it. According to the Kufans, it is the direct object (maf'ul bihi). In His saying ﴿except a little﴾ there is evidence that the excepted quantity may be unspecified, as in His saying ﴿they did not do it, except a few of them﴾ according to the reading of the one who put the word in the accusative in ﴿then you turned away, except a few of you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 83]. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: "The little is less than a tenth and a sixth." Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: "[p. 361] A third." It was also said: "Less than half." They allowed that its half (nisfahu) could be a substitute (badal) of al-layl and of qalilan. If it is a substitute for al-layl, the exception is from it, and the one commanded to stand is half the night except a little of it. The pronoun in minhu and 'alayhi returns to the half, so the meaning becomes: "Stand for half the night except a little, or reduce a little from half the night, or add to half the night." Then His saying "or reduce from half the night a little" would be a repetition of His saying "except a little of half the night," and that is a construction that is not eloquent, from which the Qur'an is free.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Nisfahu is a substitute for al-layl, and ﴿except a little﴾ is an exception from the half, as if He said: 'Stand less than half the night.' The pronoun in minhu and 'alayhi refers to the half, and the meaning is an option between two things: between standing less than half the night as a firm decision, and between choosing one of the two, which are reducing from the half and adding to it." End of quote. He did not notice the repetition that this view entails, because on his reading, "stand less than half the night" would make His saying "or reduce from half the night" a repetition. If nisfahu is a substitute for ﴿except a little﴾, the pronoun in nisfahu either returns to the substituted noun or to the excepted noun, which is al-layl. It cannot return to the substituted noun, because that would turn it into an exception of an unknown from an unknown, since the sense would be "except a little, the half of the little," and that has no meaning at all. If the pronoun returns to al-layl, then there is no benefit in the exception from al-layl, since the construction "stand at night, half of it" would be shorter, clearer, and further from ambiguity. We have already refuted the view of those who said: "except a little" is an exception from the substitute, which is its half, and that the sense is "stand at night, half of it, except a little of it," meaning of the half. Also, in the claim that nisfahu is a substitute for ﴿except a little﴾, with the pronoun in ﴿nisfahu﴾ returning to al-layl, there is the application of the word "little" to half, and it would also follow that the sense becomes "except half of it, so do not stand for it, or reduce from the half you do not stand for, or add to it the half you do not stand for." This meaning is not valid, and it is certainly not the intent of the verse.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: "If you wish, you may make nisfahu a substitute for qalilan, and it would be an option between three things: between standing for the half in full, between standing for less than the half, and between standing for more than the half. He described the half as little only in relation to the whole. If you wish, you may say: since the meaning of ﴿stand at night, except a little﴾ ﴿half of it﴾ is, when you make the half a substitute for al-layl, 'stand less than half the night,' the pronoun in minhu and 'alayhi returns to the lesser of the half, so it is as if it were said: 'Stand less than half the night, and stand less than that, except a little less or a little more than it.' The option then lies beyond the half, between it and the third. It is also permissible, if you make nisfahu a substitute for qalilan and interpret it by it, to make the second qalilan mean half of the half, which is a quarter, as if it were said: 'or reduce from it a little, its half,' and to make the addition to this little, meaning the quarter, half of the quarter, as if it were said: 'or add to it a little, its half.' It is also permissible to make the addition, since it is unrestricted, complete the third, so that it becomes an option between the half, the third, and the quarter." End of quote. How wide this man's imagination is! He permits what is close and what is far, but the Qur'an should not be taken in this way. Rather, it must not be interpreted except in the best of the ways found in Arabic speech, as we have explained in the introduction to this book. Among those who stated that nisfahu may be a substitute for al-layl or for qalilan is al-Zamakhshari, as we quoted from him. Ibn Atiyyah mentioned it as a possibility. Abu al-Baqa said: "The more likely reading of the apparent meaning of the verse is that it is a substitute for qalilan, and ﴿or add to it﴾, with the pronoun in both referring to the half. If the exception were from the half, the sense would become: 'Stand half the night except a little, or reduce from it a little.' The excepted little is not determined, so reducing from it cannot be realised." End of quote. As for al-Hawfi, he permitted it to be a substitute for "al-layl" and mentioned no other possibility.

Ibn Atiyyah said: "It may be, in my view, that His saying ﴿except a little﴾ is an exception from the standing, so that al-layl is taken as a generic noun. Then He said: ﴿except a little﴾, meaning the nights in which one is excused from standing because of a clear excuse and the like. This view is good with the opinion that it is recommended." End of quote. This is contrary to the apparent meaning. It was also said: the meaning is "or half of it," as you say: "Give him a dirham, two dirhams, three dirhams," meaning "or two dirhams, or three." End of quote. In this there is the omission of the conjunction without any indication of it.

Al-Tibrizi said: "The command to stand and the option of adding or reducing fall upon two-thirds of the last part of the night, because the first third is the time of 'atamah (the late evening prayer). The exception applies to what is commanded, so it is as if He said: 'Stand two-thirds of the night except a little.' Then He made nisfahu a substitute for qalilan, so the little becomes explained as half of the two-thirds, which is a little of the whole. So His saying ﴿or reduce from it﴾ means from what is commanded, which is standing for the two-thirds. ﴿A little﴾ means less than half of it, ﴿or add to it﴾ means to the two-thirds, so the option of adding and reducing falls upon the two-thirds." Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: "People have said a great deal about the interpretation of this verse. In my view there are two summarised points," and he mentioned a long, patched-together discussion which can be found in his book. The explanation of tartil (measured, distinct recitation) has already been given at the end of surat al-Isra.

﴿A heavy word﴾: it is the Qur'an, and its heaviness lies in what it contains of heavy obligations, such as jihad and constant good deeds. Al-Hasan said: "Reciting quickly is light, but the action is heavy." Abu al-Aliyah and al-Qurtubi said: "Its heaviness is upon the disbelievers and the hypocrites, through its inimitability and its warning." It was also said: its heaviness is what would befall his body, peace be upon him, at the time of receiving revelation, to the extent that his camel would kneel with him at that time, and his noble head would almost crush the thigh of Zayd ibn Thabit. It was also said: it is speech that has weight and gravity, not frivolous. Ibn Abbas said: "A great word." It was also said: it is heavy in the balance on the Day of Resurrection, and this is an indication of acting upon it. It was also said: it is a metaphor for its remaining over the course of time, because what is heavy by nature stays in its place.

**In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.**

*Tazammala fī thawbihi*: he wrapped himself up in his garment, i.e., covered himself. *Zamala*: he wrapped. Imru' al-Qays said:

*Kabīru unāsin fī bijādin muzammali*
(a chief of people wrapped in a coarse cloak)

Dhu al-Rumma said:

*Wa-kā'inin takhaṭṭat nāqatī min mafāzatin wa-min nā'imin 'an laylihā mutazammili*
(And how many a one my she-camel has passed over from a desert, and from a sleeper wrapped up, heedless of its night.)

*Tabattala ilā kadhā*: he devoted himself to it, cut himself off towards it. From this comes *hibatun batlatun* (an unconditional gift) and *ṭalqatun batlatun* (an irrevocable divorce). Also *al-batūl* and *batala al-ḥabl* (he cut the rope). Al-Layth said: *al-batl* is distinguishing one thing from another. *Al-batūl* is a woman cut off from men, having no desire for them and no need of them. *Al-tabattul* is abandoning marriage and renouncing it. From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*Tuḍī' al-ẓalāma bi-l-'ishā'i ka-annahā ∗∗∗ manāratu mumsā rāhibin mutabattili*
(She lights up the darkness at nightfall as though she were the lamp of a monk, at evening, devoted to solitude.)

From it is the prohibition of *tabattul*, i.e., of abstaining from marriage. From this the monk is called *mutabattil*, because he cuts himself off from people and withdraws to worship. *Al-ghuṣṣa*: the choking, which is what lodges in the throat from a bone or something else. Its plural is *ghuṣaṣ*. The verb is *ghaṣiṣta*, so you are *ghāṣṣ* and *ghaṣṣān*. He said:

*Kuntu ka-l-ghaṣṣāni bi-l-mā'i i'tiṣārī*
(I was like one choking on water while I drank.)

*Al-kathīb*: the gathered sand. Its plural is *kuthub* and *kuthbān* for many, and *akthibah* for few. Dhu al-Rumma said:

*Faqultu lahā lā inna ahlī jīratun ∗∗∗ li-akthibati al-dahnā jamī'an wa-māliyā*
(I said to her: No, indeed my family are neighbours to the dunes of al-Dahnā, all of them, and so is my property.)

*Al-mahīl*: that which gives way under a man's foot. *Hiltu 'alayhi al-turāb*: I poured the earth over it. Al-Kalbī said: *al-mahīl* is that which, when a foot treads on it, slips from beneath it, and when its base is seized, it collapses. *Ahaltu* is a dialectal variant of *hiltu*. *Al-shīb*: plural of *ashyab* (grey-haired).

This surah is entirely Meccan, according to al-Ḥasan, ʿIkrima, ʿAṭāʾ and Jābir. Ubayy (Ubayy ibn Ka'b) recited (al-mutazammil) in its original form. Ikrimah recited it with the zay lightened, meaning "the one who wraps his body or himself." Some of the early scholars (al-salaf) recited it with the zay lightened and the mim fathah, meaning "the one who has been wrapped." Al-Zamakhshari has a discussion on how God called him with this description, but I struck it out and left it out of my book. Al-Suhayli said: "al-Muzzammil is not one of his names, peace be upon him, by which he is known. It is derived from the state he was in at the time of being addressed. When the Arabs wish to show tenderness to the one they address and leave out reproach, they call him by a name derived from the state he is in, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Ali, may Allah honour his face, when he was asleep and dust was clinging to his side: 'Get up, Abu Turab' (father of dust)." This indicates that he is being gentle with him. So His saying ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ contains affection and tenderness.

The majority recited ﴿qum al-layl﴾ with a kasra on the mim, following the original rule for joining two sukun letters. Abu al-Sammal recited it with a damma, to follow the vowel of the qaf. It was also read with a fathah, seeking lightness. Ibn Jinni said: "The purpose of the vowel is to avoid joining two sukun letters, so whichever vowel the letter takes achieves the aim. Qum is a command." The majority said: "It is on the basis of recommendation (nadb)." It was also said: "It was an obligation upon the Messenger alone," and it was said: "It was upon him and upon all of them." Qatadah said: "It continued for a year or two." Aisha said: "Eight months. Then Allah had mercy on them and the verse was revealed: ﴿Surely your Lord knows﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20] and the following verses, and He lightened it for them. ﴿Stand up at night, except a little.﴾"

The exception shows that the standing commanded covers the whole night, which is why the exception from it is valid. If it did not cover the whole night, the exception from it would not be valid. Standing for the whole night continuously is not possible, so He made an exception from it for the rest of the body. According to the Basrans, al-layl is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf), even though the verb covers it. According to the Kufans, it is the direct object (maf'ul bihi). In His saying ﴿except a little﴾ there is evidence that the excepted quantity may be unspecified, as in His saying ﴿they did not do it, except a few of them﴾ according to the reading of the one who put the word in the accusative in ﴿then you turned away, except a few of you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 83]. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: "The little is less than a tenth and a sixth." Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: "[p. 361] A third." It was also said: "Less than half." They allowed that its half (nisfahu) could be a substitute (badal) of al-layl and of qalilan. If it is a substitute for al-layl, the exception is from it, and the one commanded to stand is half the night except a little of it. The pronoun in minhu and 'alayhi returns to the half, so the meaning becomes: "Stand for half the night except a little, or reduce a little from half the night, or add to half the night." Then His saying "or reduce from half the night a little" would be a repetition of His saying "except a little of half the night," and that is a construction that is not eloquent, from which the Qur'an is free.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Nisfahu is a substitute for al-layl, and ﴿except a little﴾ is an exception from the half, as if He said: 'Stand less than half the night.' The pronoun in minhu and 'alayhi refers to the half, and the meaning is an option between two things: between standing less than half the night as a firm decision, and between choosing one of the two, which are reducing from the half and adding to it." End of quote. He did not notice the repetition that this view entails, because on his reading, "stand less than half the night" would make His saying "or reduce from half the night" a repetition. If nisfahu is a substitute for ﴿except a little﴾, the pronoun in nisfahu either returns to the substituted noun or to the excepted noun, which is al-layl. It cannot return to the substituted noun, because that would turn it into an exception of an unknown from an unknown, since the sense would be "except a little, the half of the little," and that has no meaning at all. If the pronoun returns to al-layl, then there is no benefit in the exception from al-layl, since the construction "stand at night, half of it" would be shorter, clearer, and further from ambiguity. We have already refuted the view of those who said: "except a little" is an exception from the substitute, which is its half, and that the sense is "stand at night, half of it, except a little of it," meaning of the half. Also, in the claim that nisfahu is a substitute for ﴿except a little﴾, with the pronoun in ﴿nisfahu﴾ returning to al-layl, there is the application of the word "little" to half, and it would also follow that the sense becomes "except half of it, so do not stand for it, or reduce from the half you do not stand for, or add to it the half you do not stand for." This meaning is not valid, and it is certainly not the intent of the verse.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: "If you wish, you may make nisfahu a substitute for qalilan, and it would be an option between three things: between standing for the half in full, between standing for less than the half, and between standing for more than the half. He described the half as little only in relation to the whole. If you wish, you may say: since the meaning of ﴿stand at night, except a little﴾ ﴿half of it﴾ is, when you make the half a substitute for al-layl, 'stand less than half the night,' the pronoun in minhu and 'alayhi returns to the lesser of the half, so it is as if it were said: 'Stand less than half the night, and stand less than that, except a little less or a little more than it.' The option then lies beyond the half, between it and the third. It is also permissible, if you make nisfahu a substitute for qalilan and interpret it by it, to make the second qalilan mean half of the half, which is a quarter, as if it were said: 'or reduce from it a little, its half,' and to make the addition to this little, meaning the quarter, half of the quarter, as if it were said: 'or add to it a little, its half.' It is also permissible to make the addition, since it is unrestricted, complete the third, so that it becomes an option between the half, the third, and the quarter." End of quote. How wide this man's imagination is! He permits what is close and what is far, but the Qur'an should not be taken in this way. Rather, it must not be interpreted except in the best of the ways found in Arabic speech, as we have explained in the introduction to this book. Among those who stated that nisfahu may be a substitute for al-layl or for qalilan is al-Zamakhshari, as we quoted from him. Ibn Atiyyah mentioned it as a possibility. Abu al-Baqa said: "The more likely reading of the apparent meaning of the verse is that it is a substitute for qalilan, and ﴿or add to it﴾, with the pronoun in both referring to the half. If the exception were from the half, the sense would become: 'Stand half the night except a little, or reduce from it a little.' The excepted little is not determined, so reducing from it cannot be realised." End of quote. As for al-Hawfi, he permitted it to be a substitute for "al-layl" and mentioned no other possibility.

Ibn Atiyyah said: "It may be, in my view, that His saying ﴿except a little﴾ is an exception from the standing, so that al-layl is taken as a generic noun. Then He said: ﴿except a little﴾, meaning the nights in which one is excused from standing because of a clear excuse and the like. This view is good with the opinion that it is recommended." End of quote. This is contrary to the apparent meaning. It was also said: the meaning is "or half of it," as you say: "Give him a dirham, two dirhams, three dirhams," meaning "or two dirhams, or three." End of quote. In this there is the omission of the conjunction without any indication of it.

Al-Tibrizi said: "The command to stand and the option of adding or reducing fall upon two-thirds of the last part of the night, because the first third is the time of 'atamah (the late evening prayer). The exception applies to what is commanded, so it is as if He said: 'Stand two-thirds of the night except a little.' Then He made nisfahu a substitute for qalilan, so the little becomes explained as half of the two-thirds, which is a little of the whole. So His saying ﴿or reduce from it﴾ means from what is commanded, which is standing for the two-thirds. ﴿A little﴾ means less than half of it, ﴿or add to it﴾ means to the two-thirds, so the option of adding and reducing falls upon the two-thirds." Abu Abdullah al-Razi said: "People have said a great deal about the interpretation of this verse. In my view there are two summarised points," and he mentioned a long, patched-together discussion which can be found in his book. The explanation of tartil (measured, distinct recitation) has already been given at the end of surat al-Isra.

﴿A heavy word﴾: it is the Qur'an, and its heaviness lies in what it contains of heavy obligations, such as jihad and constant good deeds. Al-Hasan said: "Reciting quickly is light, but the action is heavy." Abu al-Aliyah and al-Qurtubi said: "Its heaviness is upon the disbelievers and the hypocrites, through its inimitability and its warning." It was also said: its heaviness is what would befall his body, peace be upon him, at the time of receiving revelation, to the extent that his camel would kneel with him at that time, and his noble head would almost crush the thigh of Zayd ibn Thabit. It was also said: it is speech that has weight and gravity, not frivolous. Ibn Abbas said: "A great word." It was also said: it is heavy in the balance on the Day of Resurrection, and this is an indication of acting upon it. It was also said: it is a metaphor for its remaining over the course of time, because what is heavy by nature stays in its place.

The exception shows that the standing commanded covers the whole night, which is why the exception from it is valid. If it did not cover the whole night, the exception from it would not be valid. Standing for the whole night continuously is not possible, so He made an exception from it for the rest of the body. According to the Basrans, al-layl is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf), even though the verb covers it. According to the Kufans, it is the direct object (maf'ul bihi). In His saying ﴿except a little﴾ there is evidence that the excepted quantity may be unspecified, as in His saying ﴿they did not do it, except a few of them﴾ according to the reading of the one who put the word in the accusative in ﴿then you turned away, except a few of you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 83]. They allowed that its half (nisfahu) could be a substitute (badal) of al-layl and of qalilan. If it is a substitute for al-layl, the exception is from it, and the one commanded to stand is half the night except a little of it. The pronoun in minhu and 'alayhi returns to the half, so the meaning becomes: "Stand for half the night except a little, or reduce a little from half the night, or add to half the night." Then His saying "or reduce from half the night a little" would be a repetition of His saying "except a little of half the night," and that is a construction that is not eloquent, from which the Qur'an is free.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Nisfahu is a substitute for al-layl, and ﴿except a little﴾ is an exception from the half, as if He said: 'Stand less than half the night.' The pronoun in minhu and 'alayhi refers to the half, and the meaning is an option between two things: between standing less than half the night as a firm decision, and between choosing one of the two, which are reducing from the half and adding to it." End of quote. He did not notice the repetition that this view entails, because on his reading, "stand less than half the night" would make His saying "or reduce from half the night" a repetition. If nisfahu is a substitute for ﴿except a little﴾, the pronoun in nisfahu either returns to the substituted noun or to the excepted noun, which is al-layl. It cannot return to the substituted noun, because that would turn it into an exception of an unknown from an unknown, since the sense would be "except a little, the half of the little," and that has no meaning at all. If the pronoun returns to al-layl, then there is no benefit in the exception from al-layl, since the construction "stand at night, half of it" would be shorter, clearer, and further from ambiguity. We have already refuted the view of those who said: "except a little" is an exception from the substitute, which is its half, and that the sense is "stand at night, half of it, except a little of it," meaning of the half. Also, in the claim that nisfahu is a substitute for ﴿except a little﴾, with the pronoun in ﴿nisfahu﴾ returning to al-layl, there is the application of the word "little" to half, and it would also follow that the sense becomes "except half of it, so do not stand for it, or reduce from the half you do not stand for, or add to it the half you do not stand for." This meaning is not valid, and it is certainly not the intent of the verse.

Al-Zamakhshari also said: "If you wish, you may make nisfahu a substitute for qalilan, and it would be an option between three things: between standing for the half in full, between standing for less than the half, and between standing for more than the half. He described the half as little only in relation to the whole. If you wish, you may say: since the meaning of ﴿stand at night, except a little﴾ ﴿half of it﴾ is, when you make the half a substitute for al-layl, 'stand less than half the night,' the pronoun in minhu and 'alayhi returns to the lesser of the half, so it is as if it were said: 'Stand less than half the night, and stand less than that, except a little less or a little more than it.' The option then lies beyond the half, between it and the third. It is also permissible, if you make nisfahu a substitute for qalilan and interpret it by it, to make the second qalilan mean half of the half, which is a quarter, as if it were said: 'or reduce from it a little, its half,' and to make the addition to this little, meaning the quarter, half of the quarter, as if it were said: 'or add to it a little, its half.' It is also permissible to make the addition, since it is unrestricted, complete the third, so that it becomes an option between the half, the third, and the quarter." End of quote. How wide this man's imagination is! He permits what is close and what is far, but the Qur'an should not be taken in this way. Rather, it must not be interpreted except in the best of the ways found in Arabic speech, as we have explained in the introduction to this book. Among those who stated that nisfahu may be a substitute for al-layl or for qalilan is al-Zamakhshari, as we quoted from him. Ibn Atiyyah mentioned it as a possibility. Abu al-Baqa said: "The more likely reading of the apparent meaning of the verse is that it is a substitute for qalilan, and ﴿or add to it﴾, with the pronoun in both referring to the half. The excepted little is not determined, so reducing from it cannot be realised." End of quote. As for al-Hawfi, he permitted it to be a substitute for "al-layl" and mentioned no other possibility.

Ibn Atiyyah said: "It may be, in my view, that His saying ﴿except a little﴾ is an exception from the standing, so that al-layl is taken as a generic noun. End of quote. This is contrary to the apparent meaning. It was also said: the meaning is "or half of it," as you say: "Give him a dirham, two dirhams, three dirhams," meaning "or two dirhams, or three." End of quote. In this there is the omission of the conjunction without any indication of it.

Al-Tibrizi said: "The command to stand and the option of adding or reducing fall upon two-thirds of the last part of the night, because the first third is the time of 'atamah (the late evening prayer). Then He made nisfahu a substitute for qalilan, so the little becomes explained as half of the two-thirds, which is a little of the whole. In my view there are two summarised points," and he mentioned a long, patched-together discussion which can be found in his book. The explanation of tartil (measured, distinct recitation) has already been given at the end of surat al-Isra.

﴿A heavy word﴾: it is the Qur'an, and its heaviness lies in what it contains of heavy obligations, such as jihad and constant good deeds. Abu al-Aliyah and al-Qurtubi said: "Its heaviness is upon the disbelievers and the hypocrites, through its inimitability and its warning." It was also said: its heaviness is what would befall his body, peace be upon him, at the time of receiving revelation, to the extent that his camel would kneel with him at that time, and his noble head would almost crush the thigh of Zayd ibn Thabit. It was also said: it is speech that has weight and gravity, not frivolous. Ibn Abbas said: "A great word." It was also said: it is heavy in the balance on the Day of Resurrection, and this is an indication of acting upon it. It was also said: it is a metaphor for its remaining over the course of time, because what is heavy by nature stays in its place.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 73, verse 6–16:

'A'isha and Mujahid said: it is standing (in prayer) after sleep; and whoever stands in prayer at the beginning of the night before sleeping has not stood in the rising of the night. Ibn Jubayr and Ibn Zayd said: it is a non-Arabic word (lafzah habashiyyah); "nasha'a al-rajul" means the man stood up from the night, so nashi'ah on this view is the plural of nashi', meaning one who stands. Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Zayd also, and a group said: nashi'at al-layl means its hours, because they arise one after another. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Hasan and Abu Mijlaz said: whatever comes after 'Isha' is nashi'ah, and whatever comes before it is not nashi'ah. Ibn 'Abbas said: their prayer used to be at the beginning of the night. He and Ibn al-Zubayr said: the whole night is nashi'ah. al-Kisa'i said: nashi'at al-layl is its beginning. al-Zamakhshari said: nashi'at al-layl is the soul that rises at night from its bed to worship, i.e., it rises and gets up, from "nasha'at al-sahabah" when the cloud rises, and "nasha'a min makanihi" and "nashar" when he gets up. The poet said:

"We rose toward lean camels, which the night journey had emaciated, and which had made the tips of their humps stick out."

Or: it is the standing of the night, on the basis that nashi'ah is a verbal noun from "nasha'a" meaning to stand and rise, on the pattern of al-'aqibah (the outcome). End of quotation.

The majority read (wiṭa'an) with a kasra on the waw and a fatha on the ta', with madd. Qatadah and Shibl, from the people of Makkah, read with a kasra on the waw and sukun on the ta', with the hamza shortened (maqsurah). Ibn Muhaysin read with a fatha on the waw, with madd. The meaning is that it is more conducive to agreement (mu'atha'ah), i.e., the heart agrees with the tongue in it, or it is more in harmony with what is desired of humility (khushu') and sincerity (ikhlas). It was said: it is more established for the action and more lasting for one who wishes to increase in worship, and the night is a time of leisure, so the worship endures.

﴿And more upright in speech (aqwamu qilan)﴾ i.e., more firmly correct, because voices are quiet, so what the one praying recites does not get jumbled. Ibn Shajarah related: quicker in responding to supplication. Zayd ibn Aslam said: more fitting for the reciter to gain understanding (yatafaqqah) in it.

The majority read (sabhan), i.e., movement and turning about in important matters, as the swimmer moves back and forth in water. The poet said:

"O friend, you have roamed the lands of east and west, and in them for you, O friend, is a swimming from swimming."

It was said: sabhan means subhah, i.e., supererogatory prayer. Ibn Ya'mur, 'Ikrimah and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read (sabkhan) with an unpointed kha', and its meaning is lightness from obligations; al-tasbikh is lightening, and it is a metaphor from sabbakha al-suf (he carded the wool) when he fluffed it and spread its parts, so its meaning is dispersal of resolve and scattering of the mind through preoccupations. It was said: leisure and spaciousness for your sleep and for your dealings with your needs. It was said: the meaning is that if the nightly portion (hizb al-layl) is missed through sleep or an excuse, then let him make it up by day, for in it there is a long sabh. This reading may bear meanings other than this, but they both interpreted it thus, so one does not go beyond it. End of quotation. "So sabbikh (lighten) your worry upon yourself, and know that when al-Rahman decrees something, it will come to pass."

al-Asma'i said: one says sabbakha Allah 'anka al-hummá, i.e., God lightened the fever from you. It was said: al-sabkh means stretching; one says "sabbikhi qutnaki," i.e., stretch it out; and pieces of cotton are called saba'ikh, the singular being sabiqah. From this is the saying of al-Akhtal:

"They sent them forth scattering the dust, as one scatters the sabaikh of cotton when the bow-strings are plucked (nadf awtar)."

﴿And mention the name of your Lord﴾ i.e., persist in remembering Him; this encompasses every remembrance, of glorification (tasbih), declaration of His oneness (tahlil) and other things. ﴿Tabtilan﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun of a form other than its root verb; what made this acceptable is that it forms the closing rhyme (fasilah). Al-Akhawan, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr and Ya'qub read (Rabbi) in the genitive as a substitute (badal) for (Rabbika). The rest of the seven read it in the nominative. Zayd ibn 'Ali read it in the accusative. The majority read ﴿al-mashriqi wal-maghrib﴾ in the singular. 'Abd Allah and his companions and Ibn 'Abbas read them in the dual. al-Zamakhshari said, and it is related from Ibn 'Abbas: it is an oath. He means: (Rabb) is in the genitive by the implied particle of oath, like your saying: "By God, I will surely do it," and its response is: "There is no god but He," just as you say: "By God, no one is in the house except Zayd." End of quotation. Perhaps this derivation is not sound from Ibn 'Abbas, since it involves the implied omission of the preposition in an oath, which according to the Basrans is permitted only with the word "Allah," and cannot be analogized upon. Also, when a negated nominal clause is the answer to an oath, it is negated only with "ma" alone, and it is negated with "la" only in the case of a clause introduced by a verb in the present tense frequently, or a past tense verb with present meaning rarely, such as the poet's saying:

"They turned back, so by God we shall never visit you, as long as there is water in our wells for a drinker."

al-Zamakhshari presented this by way of possibility and concession. What the grammarians mention is negating it with "ma," such as the saying of the poet:

"By your life, Sa'd is not a companion of a sinner, nor a hesitant one on the day of defense, nor a niggard."

﴿So take Him as Trustee (wakil)﴾, for whoever is singled out for divinity does not take a trustee other than Him. (And be patient) ﴿and forsake them with graceful forsaking﴾: it was said it is abrogated by the verse of the sword.

﴿And leave Me with the deniers﴾: it was said it was revealed concerning the chieftains of Quraysh; it was said: concerning those who fed (the Quraysh) on the day of Badr. Their names were mentioned in Surah al-Anfal, and the explanation of similar wording was given at ﴿So leave Me with whoever denies this discourse﴾ [al-Qalam: 44].

﴿Possessors of luxury (ni'mah)﴾, i.e., the ease of life and abundance of wealth and children. Ni'mah with a fatha means enjoyment; with a kasra, bounties and what is bestowed; with a damma, joy. One says: "ni'am" and "ni'mat 'ayn" (delight of the eye).

﴿And grant them respite a little﴾: a threat to them of swift retribution, and "a little" refers to the reaching of their appointed terms. It was said: it refers to the battle of Badr.

﴿Indeed with Us﴾ i.e., that which is contrary to their bounty: (ankal) fetters on their feet. al-Sha'bi said: they were not placed on their feet out of fear of their fleeing, but when they wanted to rise, they were weighed down by them. al-Kalbi said: al-ankal are shackles; the first is better known in the language, and from it is the saying of al-Khansa':

"You called, so you cut its fetters, though before you they were never cut."

(And a blazing fire) (jahiman): a fire of intense kindling.

﴿And food that chokes﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: a thorn of fire that lodges in their throats; it neither comes out nor goes down. Mujahid and others said: the tree of zaqqum. It was said: al-dari' and the tree of zaqqum. (On the Day) is in the accusative by the governing element in (ladayna), and it was said: by (dharni). (Shall quake) (tarjufu): will tremble. The majority read (tarjufu) with a fatha on the ta', in the active voice. Zayd ibn 'Ali read it with a damma, in the passive voice. ﴿Heaped-up sand (kathiban)﴾, i.e., gathered sand; ﴿flowing (mahilan)﴾, i.e., loose and soft. It was said: one says mahil and mahyul, kayl and makyul, madin and madyun; completion in the defective (dhawat al-ya') is the dialect of Tamim, and deletion is the usage of most Arabs.

When He threatened the deniers with the terrors of the Resurrection, He reminded them of the condition of Pharaoh and how God seized him, when he denied Musa (peace be upon him), and that if their denial persisted, God would destroy them. So He said: ﴿Indeed We have sent to you﴾, and the address is general to black and red alike. It was said: it is to the people of Makkah, ﴿a messenger, a witness against you﴾, as He said: ﴿And We bring you as a witness against these﴾ [al-Nahl: 89]. 'Abd Allah and his companions and Ibn 'Abbas read them in the dual. al-Zamakhshari said, and it is related from Ibn 'Abbas: it is an oath. He means: (Rabb) is in the genitive by the implied particle of oath, like your saying: "By God, I will surely do it," and its response is: "There is no god but He," just as you say: "By God, no one is in the house except Zayd." End of quotation. Perhaps this derivation is not sound from Ibn 'Abbas, since it involves the implied omission of the preposition in an oath, which according to the Basrans is permitted only with the word "Allah," and cannot be analogized upon. Also, when a negated nominal clause is the answer to an oath, it is negated only with "ma" alone, and it is negated with "la" only in the case of a clause introduced by a verb in the present tense frequently, or a past tense verb with present meaning rarely, such as the poet's saying:

"They turned back, so by God we shall never visit you, as long as there is water in our wells for a drinker."

al-Zamakhshari presented this by way of possibility and concession. What the grammarians mention is negating it with "ma," such as the saying of the poet:

"By your life, Sa'd is not a companion of a sinner, nor a hesitant one on the day of defense, nor a niggard."

﴿So take Him as Trustee (wakil)﴾, for whoever is singled out for divinity does not take a trustee other than Him. (And be patient) ﴿and forsake them with graceful forsaking﴾: it was said it is abrogated by the verse of the sword.

﴿And leave Me with the deniers﴾: it was said it was revealed concerning the chieftains of Quraysh; it was said: concerning those who fed (the Quraysh) on the day of Badr. Their names were mentioned in Surah al-Anfal, and the explanation of similar wording was given at ﴿So leave Me with whoever denies this discourse﴾ [al-Qalam: 44].

﴿Possessors of luxury (ni'mah)﴾, i.e., the ease of life and abundance of wealth and children. Ni'mah with a fatha means enjoyment; with a kasra, bounties and what is bestowed; with a damma, joy. One says: "ni'am" and "ni'mat 'ayn" (delight of the eye).

﴿And grant them respite a little﴾: a threat to them of swift retribution, and "a little" refers to the reaching of their appointed terms. It was said: it refers to the battle of Badr.

﴿Indeed with Us﴾ i.e., that which is contrary to their bounty: (ankal) fetters on their feet. al-Sha'bi said: they were not placed on their feet out of fear of their fleeing, but when they wanted to rise, they were weighed down by them. al-Kalbi said: al-ankal are shackles; the first is better known in the language, and from it is the saying of al-Khansa':

"You called, so you cut its fetters, though before you they were never cut."

(And a blazing fire) (jahiman): a fire of intense kindling.

﴿And food that chokes﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: a thorn of fire that lodges in their throats; it neither comes out nor goes down. Mujahid and others said: the tree of zaqqum. It was said: al-dari' and the tree of zaqqum. (On the Day) is in the accusative by the governing element in (ladayna), and it was said: by (dharni). (Shall quake) (tarjufu): will tremble. The majority read (tarjufu) with a fatha on the ta', in the active voice. Zayd ibn 'Ali read it with a damma, in the passive voice. ﴿Heaped-up sand (kathiban)﴾, i.e., gathered sand; ﴿flowing (mahilan)﴾, i.e., loose and soft. It was said: one says mahil and mahyul, kayl and makyul, madin and madyun; completion in the defective (dhawat al-ya') is the dialect of Tamim, and deletion is the usage of most Arabs.

When He threatened the deniers with the terrors of the Resurrection, He reminded them of the condition of Pharaoh and how God seized him, when he denied Musa (peace be upon him), and that if their denial persisted, God would destroy them. So He said: ﴿Indeed We have sent to you﴾, and the address is general to black and red alike. It was said: it is to the people of Makkah, ﴿a messenger, a witness against you﴾, as He said: ﴿And We bring you as a witness against these﴾ [al-Nahl: 89]. He likened the sending to the people of Makkah to the sending of Musa to Pharaoh specifically, because each of them grew up among his people and was despised by them, and they had knowledge of what befell Pharaoh by drowning, so it was fitting to liken the sending to the sending. It was said: "the messenger" carries the definite article because its mention had preceded, so it refers back to it, as you say: "I met a man and I struck the man," because the one struck is the one met. And al-wabil means the evil in outcome, from the saying of them: "kala' wabil," i.e., unwholesome, not digestible because of its heaviness, meaning it does not settle in the gullet.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 73, verse 6–16:

'A'isha and Mujahid said: it is standing (in prayer) after sleep; and whoever stands in prayer at the beginning of the night before sleeping has not stood in the rising of the night. Ibn Jubayr and Ibn Zayd said: it is a non-Arabic word (lafzah habashiyyah); "nasha'a al-rajul" means the man stood up from the night, so nashi'ah on this view is the plural of nashi', meaning one who stands. Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Zayd also, and a group said: nashi'at al-layl means its hours, because they arise one after another. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Hasan and Abu Mijlaz said: whatever comes after 'Isha' is nashi'ah, and whatever comes before it is not nashi'ah. Ibn 'Abbas said: their prayer used to be at the beginning of the night. He and Ibn al-Zubayr said: the whole night is nashi'ah. al-Kisa'i said: nashi'at al-layl is its beginning. al-Zamakhshari said: nashi'at al-layl is the soul that rises at night from its bed to worship, i.e., it rises and gets up, from "nasha'at al-sahabah" when the cloud rises, and "nasha'a min makanihi" and "nashar" when he gets up. The poet said:

"We rose toward lean camels, which the night journey had emaciated, and which had made the tips of their humps stick out."

Or: it is the standing of the night, on the basis that nashi'ah is a verbal noun from "nasha'a" meaning to stand and rise, on the pattern of al-'aqibah (the outcome). End of quotation.

The majority read (wiṭa'an) with a kasra on the waw and a fatha on the ta', with madd. Qatadah and Shibl, from the people of Makkah, read with a kasra on the waw and sukun on the ta', with the hamza shortened (maqsurah). Ibn Muhaysin read with a fatha on the waw, with madd. The meaning is that it is more conducive to agreement (mu'atha'ah), i.e., the heart agrees with the tongue in it, or it is more in harmony with what is desired of humility (khushu') and sincerity (ikhlas). As for one who reads (wat'an), meaning: firmer footing and further from slipping, or heavier and harder on the one praying than daytime prayer, as in the report: "O God, tighten Your grip (wat'ataka) upon Mudar." al-Akhfash said: more firm in standing. al-Farra' said: more established in recitation and standing. al-Kalbi said: more energetic for the one praying, because it is at the time of his rest. It was said: it is more established for the action and more lasting for one who wishes to increase in worship, and the night is a time of leisure, so the worship endures.

﴿And more upright in speech (aqwamu qilan)﴾ i.e., more firmly correct, because voices are quiet, so what the one praying recites does not get jumbled. Qatadah and Mujahid said: more right for recitation and more established for speech, because it is a time of understanding. 'Ikrimah said: more complete in energy, sincerity and blessing. Ibn Shajarah related: quicker in responding to supplication. Zayd ibn Aslam said: more fitting for the reciter to gain understanding (yatafaqqah) in it.

The majority read (sabhan), i.e., movement and turning about in important matters, as the swimmer moves back and forth in water. The poet said:

"O friend, you have roamed the lands of east and west, and in them for you, O friend, is a swimming from swimming."

It was said: sabhan means subhah, i.e., supererogatory prayer. Ibn Ya'mur, 'Ikrimah and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read (sabkhan) with an unpointed kha', and its meaning is lightness from obligations; al-tasbikh is lightening, and it is a metaphor from sabbakha al-suf (he carded the wool) when he fluffed it and spread its parts, so its meaning is dispersal of resolve and scattering of the mind through preoccupations. It was said: leisure and spaciousness for your sleep and for your dealings with your needs. It was said: the meaning is that if the nightly portion (hizb al-layl) is missed through sleep or an excuse, then let him make it up by day, for in it there is a long sabh. The author of al-Lawami said: Ibn Ya'mur and 'Ikrimah interpreted sabkhan with a pointed kha', and said: sleep, i.e., you sleep by day so that you may be strengthened by it for standing at night. This reading may bear meanings other than this, but they both interpreted it thus, so one does not go beyond it. End of quotation. In a hadith: "Do not sabbakhi (lighten) your supplication," i.e., do not make it lighter. The poet said:

"So sabbikh (lighten) your worry upon yourself, and know that when al-Rahman decrees something, it will come to pass."

al-Asma'i said: one says sabbakha Allah 'anka al-hummá, i.e., God lightened the fever from you. It was said: al-sabkh means stretching; one says "sabbikhi qutnaki," i.e., stretch it out; and pieces of cotton are called saba'ikh, the singular being sabiqah. From this is the saying of al-Akhtal:

"They sent them forth scattering the dust, as one scatters the sabaikh of cotton when the bow-strings are plucked (nadf awtar)."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 73, verses 17–20 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿How, then, will you guard yourselves, if you disbelieve, against a Day that will make children grey-haired?﴾ ﴿The sky will be split by it; His promise is ever fulfilled.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this is a reminder, so whoever wills may take a path to his Lord.﴾ ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand (in prayer) nearly two-thirds of the night, or half of it, or a third of it, and so too a group of those with you. And Allah measures the night and the day. He knows that you will not be able to keep count of it, so He has turned to you in forgiveness. So recite whatever is easy for you of the Qur'an. He knows that there will be among you those who are ill, and others who travel through the land seeking of Allah's bounty, and others who fight in the cause of Allah. So recite whatever is easy of it, establish the prayer, give the zakah, and lend to Allah a goodly loan. Whatever good you send forward for yourselves, you will find it with Allah, better and greater in reward. And seek forgiveness from Allah; indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.﴾

(Yawman) is in the accusative, governed by (tattaqun) (you guard yourselves). It is in the accusative as an object by way of metaphor, meaning: How will you face this great Day, whose nature is such-and-such? The pronoun in (yajʿalu) (makes) refers to the Day; the act of making is attributed to it because it is metaphorically the place where it occurs. Al-Zamakhshari said: (yawman) is a direct object, meaning: How will you guard yourselves on the Day of Resurrection and its terror, if you remain in disbelief, and do not believe and do righteous deeds? End of quote. (Tattaqun) is the present tense of ittaqa (to guard oneself, to fear), and ittaqa is not in the sense of waqa (to protect), such that it would be explained by it. Ittaqa is transitive to one object, while waqa is transitive to two. Allah says: ﴿And He protected them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire﴾ [al-Dukhan: 56]. For this reason al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: you protect yourselves on the Day of Resurrection, but (tattaqun) is not in the sense of (taqun), so it does not take its object. He also slipped Mu'tazili doctrine into his statement: and do not believe and do righteous deeds. He said: It is also permissible for it to be an adverbial of time, meaning: How will you have taqwa on the Day of Resurrection if you disbelieve in this world? He said: It is also permissible for it to be governed by (kafartum) (you disbelieve) under the interpretation of (jahadtum) (you deny), meaning: How will you guard yourselves, fearing Allah, if you deny on the Day of Resurrection? And the recompense, because taqwa of Allah is fear of His punishment. End of quote.

The majority read (yawman) with tanwin, and (yajʿalu) with the letter ya'. The clause (yajʿalu) is a description of (yawman). If the pronoun in (yajʿalu) refers to the Day, it is clear, and this is the apparent meaning. If it refers to Allah, as some have said, then a pronoun referring to the Day must be omitted, meaning: (yajʿalu fīhi) (makes [it] therein), like His saying: ﴿a Day when no soul will avail another at all﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48]. Zayd ibn ʿAli read without tanwin, with the letter nun: (najʿalu), so the adverbial time is a noun joined to the clause, and (al-shīb) (grey hair) is the second object of (yajʿala), meaning: the children become old men; and this is a metaphor for the severity of that Day. It is said of a severe day: a day that greys the forelocks of children. The origin of this is that when worries intensify, they quickly bring about greyness. Al-Mutanabbi said:

Worry wears down the stout, leaving them thin, and greys the forelock of the boy and makes him decrepit.

Some said: this is literal, that their heads turn grey from the intensity of the terror, just as greyness is seen in this world from excessive worry, like the anguish of the sea and the like. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible for the Day to be described as long, and that the children reach the age of old age within it.

Al-Suddi said: (al-wildan) (children) means children born of fornication. It is said: they are the children of polytheists. The apparent meaning is generality: the young one greys without having grown old, and that is when it is said to Adam: "O Adam, rise and send forth the company of the Fire." It is also said: this is the time of terror before the Trumpet is blown with the blast of annihilation.

﴿The sky will be split by it﴾. Al-Farra' said: it means the canopy; it is both masculine and feminine, so (munfatirun) is in the masculine form, and from it is the saying of the poet:

If the sky were to raise a people to Him, we would rise with the sky and with the clouds.

On the feminine reading, Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: it is of the category of the scattered locust, the green tree, and the uprooted trunks of palm. End of quote. He means that it is of the category of collective nouns whose singular is formed with the feminine ta', and that its singular is sama', and a collective noun may be treated as masculine or feminine, so (munfatir) came in the masculine. Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla', Abu ʿUbayda and al-Kisa'i, and al-Qadi Mundhir ibn Sa'id, who followed them, said: its figurative sense is the ceiling, so (munfatir) came accordingly, and he did not say (munfatirah). Abu ʿAli also said: the implied sense is "possessing splitting," like their saying: "a nursing woman" (murdi'), meaning one possessing nursing, so it proceeds by way of attribution. Al-Zamakhshari said: or the sky is a thing that is split, so he made (munfatir) a description of a supposed predicate of masculine form, which is (shay') (thing). Splitting (infitar) means cleaving and rupturing. The pronoun in (bihi) apparently refers to the Day, and the preposition (bi) indicates cause, meaning: because of the severity of that Day; or it is adverbial, meaning: within it. Mujahid said: it refers to Allah, meaning: by His command and authority. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in (wa'duhu) (His promise) refers to the Day, so it is an annexation of the verbal noun to its object, meaning: He, may He be Exalted, promised His servants this Day, which is the Day of Resurrection, so it must be fulfilled. It is also permissible for it to refer to Allah, Exalted, and then it is an annexation of the verbal noun to its subject, even though no nearby mention has preceded, because it is known that the One whose promises these are is Allah, Exalted.

(Inna hadhihi) (Indeed, this) refers to the surah, or to the shackles and what is joined to them, and the severe punishment, or to the verses of the Qur'an that contain the severity of the Resurrection (tadhkirah) (a reminder), meaning: an admonition. ﴿so whoever wills may take a path to his Lord﴾, by drawing near to Him through obedience. The object of (shā'a) (wills) is omitted, indicated by the conditional, because "man" (whoever) is conditional, meaning: whoever wills to take a path, he takes it to his Lord. The willing here is not in the sense of permission, but includes the meaning of promise and warning.

﴿Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand (in prayer) nearly...﴾: that is, you pray, like His saying: ﴿Stand [in prayer] through the night﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 2]. Since most states of prayer involve standing, He expressed prayer by it. This verse was revealed as a relief from the continuous practice of standing in prayer at night, either as obligatory or as recommended, according to the disagreement mentioned earlier.

﴿nearly two-thirds of the night﴾, meaning: for a period that is less than two-thirds of the night. The word "nearer" (adnā), which is nearest to the first, is used figuratively, because when the distance between two things is close, the space between them is small, and when it is far, that space is great. The majority read ﴿thuluthay﴾ with a damma on the lam. Al-Hasan, Shayba, Abu Haywa, Ibn al-Sumayqaʿ, Hisham and Ibn Mujahid, from Qunbul, as reported by the author of al-Kamil, read it with the lam sukun; and it is reported from Nafi' and Ibn ʿAmir, as reported by the author of al-Lawami. The two ʿArabī readers (Abu ʿAmr and al-Kisa'i) and Nafi' read ﴿nisfahu wa thuluthahu﴾ in the genitive, in conjunction with ﴿thuluthay al-layl﴾. The rest of the seven and Zayd ibn ʿAli read them in the accusative, in conjunction with (adnā), since it is accusative as an adverbial, meaning: a time nearer than two-thirds of the night. The accusative reading suits the division at the beginning of the surah: for when he stands at night except a little, it applies to him ﴿nearer than two-thirds of the night﴾, because the time in which he did not stand is a third and something of the two-thirds, so the phrase "except a little" applies to it. As for His saying ﴿half of it﴾, it corresponds to His earlier saying "half of it" (nisfah). As for ﴿a third of it﴾, His saying ﴿or reduce from it a little﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 3] may reach, in little reductions, the point where the time is a third of the night. As for His saying ﴿or add to it﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 4], when he adds a little beyond half, the time becomes less than two-thirds, so it corresponds to His saying ﴿nearer than two-thirds of the night﴾, and His saying: ﴿half of it, or reduce from it a little﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 3] serves as an explanation of what was implied by His saying: ﴿Stand [in prayer] through the night, except a little﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 2]; and this is so according to the accusative reading.

Al-Hasan and Ibn Jubayr said: the meaning of (tuḥṣūhu) (you will be unable to keep count of it) is (tuṭīqūhu) (you cannot bear it). That is, Allah decreed that they would measure the time as already mentioned at the beginning of the surah, but they could not sustain its standing because of its length and difficulty, so Allah, out of His grace, lightened it for them, not because of their ignorance of the measurement and counting of the hours. As for the genitive reading, the meaning is that the standing varies: sometimes nearer to two-thirds, sometimes nearer to half, sometimes nearer to a third, because it is beyond human ability to know the exact measures of time, given the excuse of sleep. The true measuring of time belongs to Allah, Exalted, and humans cannot reckon it, that is, they cannot bear its precise measures; so He turned to them in forgiveness, that is, He brought them back from heaviness to ease, and commanded them to stand as much as was easy. On both readings His knowledge of this is according to what actually occurred from them, because they stood those measures at different times: they stood nearer to two-thirds, half and a third, and they stood nearer to half and nearer to a third, so there is no contradiction between the two readings. The majority read (wa thuluthahu) with a damma on the lam; Ibn Kathir, in the transmission of Shibl, read it with sukun. A group (read ﴿wa ṭāʾifatun﴾ as) conjoined to the pronoun hidden in "taqūmu" (you stand), and the separation between them made it good. His saying ﴿and a group of those with you﴾ is evidence that it was not obligatory upon all, for if it were obligatory, the construction would be "and those with you," unless one holds that among them some stood in their homes and some stood with him, in which case obligation for all is possible on that view.

﴿And Allah measures the night and the day﴾, meaning: He alone, Exalted, knows the measures of the hours. Al-Zamakhshari said: placing His Name, Mighty and Majestic, first as the subject, with the predicate (yuqaddiru, measures) following, indicates the meaning of exclusivity in measuring. End of quote. This is his school, though exclusivity is derived from the context of the speech, not from fronting the subject. If you say: "Zayd memorises the Qur'an" or "studies Sibawayh's book," the fronting of the subject does not indicate exclusivity. (Anna) here is the light form of the heavy one, and the pronoun in (tuḥṣūhu) apparently refers to the understood verbal noun from (yuqaddiru), meaning: that you will not be able to count the measures of the hours of night and day, you will not encompass them in reality. It is also said that the pronoun refers to the standing understood from His saying "so He has turned to you in forgiveness." It is said: this indicates that among them were some who abandoned part of what they were commanded. It is also said: He brought you back from heaviness to lightness, and from hardship to ease, and permitted you to abandon the prescribed standing.

It is in the accusative as an object by way of metaphor, meaning: How will you face this great Day, whose nature is such-and-such? The pronoun in (yajʿalu) (makes) refers to the Day; the act of making is attributed to it because it is metaphorically the place where it occurs. Al-Zamakhshari said: (yawman) is a direct object, meaning: How will you guard yourselves on the Day of Resurrection and its terror, if you remain in disbelief, and do not believe and do righteous deeds? End of quote. (Tattaqun) is the present tense of ittaqa (to guard oneself, to fear), and ittaqa is not in the sense of waqa (to protect), such that it would be explained by it. Ittaqa is transitive to one object, while waqa is transitive to two. Allah says: ﴿And He protected them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire﴾ [al-Dukhan: 56]. For this reason al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: you protect yourselves on the Day of Resurrection, but (tattaqun) is not in the sense of (taqun), so it does not take its object. He also slipped Mu'tazili doctrine into his statement: and do not believe and do righteous deeds. He said: It is also permissible for it to be an adverbial of time, meaning: How will you have taqwa on the Day of Resurrection if you disbelieve in this world? He said: It is also permissible for it to be governed by (kafartum) (you disbelieve) under the interpretation of (jahadtum) (you deny), meaning: How will you guard yourselves, fearing Allah, if you deny on the Day of Resurrection? And the recompense, because taqwa of Allah is fear of His punishment. End of quote.

The majority read (yawman) with tanwin, and (yajʿalu) with the letter ya'. The clause (yajʿalu) is a description of (yawman). If the pronoun in (yajʿalu) refers to the Day, it is clear, and this is the apparent meaning. Zayd ibn ʿAli read without tanwin, with the letter nun: (najʿalu), so the adverbial time is a noun joined to the clause, and (al-shīb) (grey hair) is the second object of (yajʿala), meaning: the children become old men; and this is a metaphor for the severity of that Day. It is said of a severe day: a day that greys the forelocks of children. The origin of this is that when worries intensify, they quickly bring about greyness. Al-Mutanabbi said:

Worry wears down the stout, leaving them thin, and greys the forelock of the boy and makes him decrepit.

Some said: this is literal, that their heads turn grey from the intensity of the terror, just as greyness is seen in this world from excessive worry, like the anguish of the sea and the like. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible for the Day to be described as long, and that the children reach the age of old age within it.

Al-Suddi said: (al-wildan) (children) means children born of fornication. It is said: they are the children of polytheists. The apparent meaning is generality: the young one greys without having grown old, and that is when it is said to Adam: "O Adam, rise and send forth the company of the Fire." It is also said: this is the time of terror before the Trumpet is blown with the blast of annihilation.

If the sky were to raise a people to Him, we would rise with the sky and with the clouds.

On the feminine reading, Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: it is of the category of the scattered locust, the green tree, and the uprooted trunks of palm. End of quote. The willing here is not in the sense of permission, but includes the meaning of promise and warning.
